spots.name: Royal Palace of Madrid
spots.label: Royal Palace

text.directions_text: From Ópera Metro station (Metro line 2, Metro line 5 and Metro line R) the palace is about 400 m on foot, to the west. Walk along Calle de Bailén to reach the Jardines de Sabatini on the north side, which is where the phone icon on the map is. From Príncipe Pío Metro station (Metro line 10, Metro line 6 and Metro line R) it is about 550 m on foot, to the south-east. The phone icon on the map is about 390 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.geographic_location: The palace stands on Calle de Bailén in the western part of central Madrid, east of the Manzanares River and close to the Plaza de Oriente. The Jardines de Sabatini run along its north side.
text.access_note: The Jardines de Sabatini are a free public park, but the area around the Cornisa can close for events, so check the official site before you go.
text.description: The Royal Palace of Madrid is the official residence of the Spanish royal family, though it is used mainly for state ceremonies rather than as a home. It is also the largest palace in Western Europe, with 3,418 rooms. The Alcázar, built on the site of a Muslim-era fortress, burned down on Christmas Eve 1734, and the present building went up between 1738 and 1755. The north side is where it photographs best. The Jardines de Sabatini lie along that facade, on ground once used for the royal stables, and their clipped hedges and still water give you a tidy, symmetrical foreground. The palace itself is built from grey granite and white limestone, so it reads as a calm, pale block against the sky and stays clear on a small screen. From the gardens you can fit the long facade, the hedges and the reflecting pool into one frame. In late afternoon the stone takes on a warm glow and the sky has more colour. Stand back from the pool so the water adds depth without crowding the picture. If you have time for a second angle, the Campo del Moro on the west side shows the palace rising above lawns and a fountain. Whichever spot you choose, take a few frames and compare them later.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade and pool together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole width of the hedges and water, and use telephoto (2x or more) for details of the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or sunset, when the stone glows and the sky has more colour. Arrive a little before dusk, as the gardens may close then.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky keeps its colour and the pale limestone does not turn white. Keep the phone level, because tilted verticals are obvious on such a formal building.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 390 m north of the subject, in Jardines de Sabatini (the phone icon on the map), and face south. On the north side of the palace, reached along Calle de Bailén.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the palace centred, so the symmetry of the hedges and pool looks deliberate. Crouch a little to bring the water into the lower part of the frame. For a different view, the Campo del Moro shows the palace's western facade above the lawns, and you can often frame it to keep trees out.

spots.name: Puerta del Sol
spots.label: Puerta del Sol

text.directions_text: Take the Metro to Sol Metro station (Metro line 1, Metro line 2 or Metro line 3). The phone icon on the map is on the west side of the square, only a minute or so from the station exits. From there, the bear statue is about 1 minute on foot to the east. Sevilla Metro station (Metro line 2) is also close, about 4 minutes on foot, with the square to the west. The phone icon on the map is about 110 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.geographic_location: Puerta del Sol is in the very centre of Madrid, in the old town. The Plaza Mayor is just to the southwest, and the Palacio Real is further west.
text.access_note: This is an open public square, pedestrianised since 2020; no ticket is needed to take photos here, but check the official site before you go if you plan to visit any building around it.
text.description: Puerta del Sol is one of Madrid's best-known and busiest squares, and it is easy to see why people photograph it. The plaza opens out in a gentle semicircle, with the old Post Office (the Casa de Correos) and its clock tower closing the view. The name means "Gate of the Sun". It comes from a gate in Madrid's 15th-century city wall, which faced east and was decorated with a rising sun. The clock is the one whose bells mark the Twelve Grapes at New Year. The Post Office building was designed by Jacques Marquet and built between 1766 and 1768. Set into the pavement in front of it is the Km 0 plaque, the point from which Spain's road distances are measured. On the east side of the square, the bronze bear reaching up to the strawberry tree is the symbol of Madrid. Until 2009 it stood on the north side, so check its exact position on the map. Since 2020 the square has been pedestrianised, so you can step back and frame your shot without worrying about traffic. The most popular photo is taken from the west end, where you enter from Calle del Arenal, looking east across the plaza to the clock tower. The square is almost always crowded, so go early in the morning if you want a cleaner shot. A second good picture is the bear with the busy square behind it.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole square. Use the default lens (1x) for the bear and the Km 0 plaque. Try telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the clock tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the square is relatively empty and the low eastern sun lights the Casa de Correos.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the clock tower to focus and lower the exposure slider a little if the sky looks washed out. At the ultra-wide setting, keep people out of the edges of the frame, where faces can look stretched. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 110 m west of the subject, in Puerta del Sol (the phone icon on the map), and face east. From here you look east across the semicircular plaza, with the Casa de Correos clock tower as the backdrop. The bear statue is to the east of this spot, so walk over to it for a closer shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the clock tower up with the centre of the frame. Keep the horizon level so the buildings do not lean. For a second picture, go to the bear and frame it against the square's activity. Or find the Km 0 plaque in the pavement with the Casa de Correos building behind it.

spots.alt: Puerta del Sol, Madrid: one of Madrid's best-known and busiest squares. Photo spot

spots.name: Mercado de San Miguel
spots.label: Mercado de San Miguel

text.directions_text: From Ópera Metro station (Metro line 2, Metro line 5 and Metro line R), walk south for about 5 minutes on foot to reach the market. From La Latina Metro station (Metro line 5), walk north for about 7 minutes on foot. Head for the phone icon on the map, which is on the western side of the market, in the square. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Madrid, on Plaza de San Miguel, right next to Plaza Mayor and between Puerta del Sol and the Royal Palace.
text.access_note: The outside of the market can be photographed from the public square, but opening times and any rules for taking photos inside may change, so check the official site before you go.
text.description:
The Mercado de San Miguel is a covered market just off Plaza Mayor, and its wrought-iron and glass frame is what makes it so easy to photograph. It opened in 1916 and was designed by the Spanish architect Alfonso Dubé, who took inspiration from Les Halles in Paris. The building covers 1,764 square metres over two floors. Before it was built, the square held a 13th-century church, which was demolished in 1809, and later an open-air fish market. The market was renovated and reopened in 2009, and today it works as a gourmet tapas hall with dozens of stalls.

From outside, the big glass panels and slim iron columns give you clean lines and plenty of reflections. The best exterior shot is from the far western end of Plaza de San Miguel, where you can step back far enough to fit the whole facade into one wide frame. Go early on a weekday if you can, before tour groups arrive from Plaza Mayor. Inside, the iron and glass roof and the rows of busy stalls make good pictures too. Crowds are heaviest around midday and in the evening, so a quiet morning gives you the most room. If you want close shots of a stall or its produce, ask the vendor first.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full facade from the square. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as ironwork, lettering and the glass panels.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early on a weekday morning, before the square fills with groups. The market is busiest from about noon to 2pm and from 7pm to 9pm.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the glass, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky does not wash out. Indoors, try Night mode if the light is dim, and hold the phone steady against a pillar or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de San Miguel, right in front of the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. At the far western end of the square, and step back until the whole facade fits. The market is to the east of you from there. From this spot you can take the whole iron-and-glass front of the 1916 market hall in one wide shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the vertical iron columns up with them so the building does not lean. Keep your phone level, and leave a little space around the roof line. If you go inside as well, point the phone upwards for the iron and glass ceiling with light coming through. You can also take a wide shot along the rows of stalls to show how busy the hall is.
